newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta election focused on Europe and economy.
newsitem.headline: Malta election focused on Europe and economy.

text.p: Called to step into the embrace of the European Union or to back off into "positive neutrality", the people of Malta vote on Saturday in a general election focused on Europe and their wallets.
Prime Minister Eddie Fenech Adami and his Nationalist Party are pledged to pursue Malta's 1990 application for EU membership, arguing that this will ensure economic prosperity for the island.
"We will be able to open our doors without restriction to a market of 314 million people," said Fenech Adami, 62, in the party manifesto.
He also sees membership "providing the reassuring awareness that we have the security of a group of European countries."
Labour Party leader Alfred Sant, 48, vows to dismantle VAT (Value added Tax), a basic feature of EU membership, and in consequence withdraw Malta's application.

He says many EU rules are inapplicable to a small island and policies like that on agriculture would push up costs. "We should have a special relationship, not membership...I would like to see security, not military, cooperation, for example on drugs, contraband and the movement of people," he told Reuters.

Membership also conflicted with Malta's neutrality, said Sant, arguing that while tensions had eased in Europe these had not vanished in the Mediterranean between north and south, "especially with the growth of (Islamic) fundamentalism".
The Labour leader said his party would restructure talks with the EU "to build on what has been achieved" rather than start from scratch on the new relationship he envisages.

Campaign arguments have focused largely on the economy, and the European impact. But with no independent opinion polls and Malta's elections usually being determined by only a few thousand votes, few will forecast the outcome. But turnout, normally around 90 percent, is expected again to be high.

Fenech Adami's party warns: "The price Malta will have to pay for the withdrawal of its application for membership is far too great." It adds that EU membership could mean assistance of Lm43 million ($118 million) a year.
The Nationalist party had a three-seat majority in the outgoing 65-member parliament, has been in power since 1987 and urges the 275,000 electorate to judge it on its record.
It boast an economy, based mainly on manufacturing and tourism, growing at some six percent a year and unemployment down to 3.2 percent.
Some 80 percent of the Mediterranean island's trade is with European Union members, and Britain leads its tourist visitors.

Sant says many ordinary Maltese are struggling to cope with high prices and blames VAT for inflation. "It's officially four percent, double that of our main trading partners, and I think it is greater, closer to six or seven percent," he said.
Labour backs trade liberalisation but says the economy has been hijacked by what it terms "barons".
Sant said he believed the election would be won or lost on two factors: "VAT and corruption, I believe that drug money is getting involved," he said, without giving details.

Some 500 polling stations on Malta and the sister island of Gozo open at 8 a.m. on Saturday and close at 10 p.m. Counting should start shortly afterwards but with Malta's system of proportional representation results are not expected until late on Sunday or early on Monday.
